description: A two-part suite from Boston's 1976 debut: Tom Scholz's organ-driven instrumental 'Foreplay' crashes straight into 'Long Time,' Brad Delp's soaring vocal and all. Basement-born, arena-sized.

pops.text: It's a suite, not just a song: the instrumental 'Foreplay' runs straight into 'Long Time,' listed as a single track on the album and almost always played as one on radio.
Ancient origins: Tom Scholz said 'Foreplay' was the first piece of music he ever wrote — as far back as 1969 — and the first thing he recorded, on a two-track machine in his basement.
Scholz sang every vocal part on the basement demo himself, then invited his friend Brad Delp to try it. Delp's voice is the only one heard on the finished 1976 recording.
Solo spotlight: all three electric guitar solos on 'Long Time' are played by Barry Goudreau, while Scholz handles acoustic guitar, bass, organ and clavinet.
On 'Foreplay,' the album credits Scholz with organ, clavinet and lead guitar run through what the liner notes tease as 'top secret space pedal effects.'
The single was a tight edit: 'Long Time' was released on January 7, 1977, as Boston's second single, cut down to 3:05 from the album suite's 7:47.
Chart run: 'Long Time' peaked at No. 22 on the Billboard Hot 100 in the week ending March 5, 1977, reached No. 9 in Canada and No. 4 on the Cash Box Top 100.
'Foreplay' got a second job: the standalone instrumental turned up as the B-side of Boston's next single, 'Peace of Mind,' released in April 1977.
Rolling Stone praised the suite as 'a perfect marriage of Led Zeppelin and Yes' that plays musical chairs with electric and acoustic sounds.
Jam-band seal of approval: Phish opened their July 12, 1999 show at Great Woods in Mansfield, Massachusetts, with the full electric album version of 'Foreplay/Long Time.'

title: Foreplay / Long Time

description: The opening blast of Funkafized Plus (2012): a seven-piece Boston funk crew puts trumpet, sax, trombone and tuba where the lead singer usually stands, and grooves for five minutes.

pops.text: First impressions: 'Funkafized' opens the album Funkafized Plus, released in 2012, and sets the tone for everything after it. It runs just under five minutes, at 4:59.
The band is a seven-piece funk, jazz and soul outfit led by two founding members: trumpeter Garret Savluk and guitarist Jeff Buckridge.
The whole concept is horns first: reviewers noted the trumpet, sax, trombone and tuba players carry the core melodies instead of waiting at the side for a solo spot.
Guest firepower: celebrated soul-jazz guitarist Melvin Sparks, a longtime influence on the band, left his mark as a guest guitarist on a few of the album's tracks.
Track two is a tip of the hat: the album follows the opener with 'Sing a Simple Song,' the Sly and the Family Stone classic, recast for a horn-led band.
One groove, two servings: 'Dipper Mouth' appears on the album at track four, then returns near the middle as the shorter 'Dipper Mouth (Reprise).'
The members' résumés run deep: over the years, Boston Horns players have collaborated or toured with Tower of Power, Extreme, Susan Tedeschi and Paquito D'Rivera, among others.
The Boston Herald traced the band's roots to the soul-jazz of the late '60s and the proto-funk of the Crusaders, Tower of Power and Melvin Sparks.
The band built a following in Japan as well as Boston: their catalogue includes Live from Tokyo (2006) and Shibuya Gumbo (2007), named for Tokyo's Shibuya district.
Full-circle closer: the album's final track, 'It's in Your Face,' shares its title with the band's 1999 studio album It's In Your Face, the first entry in their catalogue.

title: Funkafized

description: Boz Scaggs' silkiest hit: a Grammy-winning slice of blue-eyed soul from Silk Degrees, built by the session players who became Toto. A Cleveland DJ broke it before the label even tried.

pops.text: It's the side-two opener on Silk Degrees (1976), Scaggs's seventh album and his commercial breakthrough, produced by Joe Wissert for Columbia Records.
Scaggs co-wrote the song with keyboardist David Paich, who also plays the Minimoog and ARP synthesizer parts you hear gliding through the track.
Meet the band that became Toto: Paich, bassist David Hungate and drummer Jeff Porcaro all played on 'Lowdown,' and touring with Scaggs helped solidify them into a band of their own.
That guitar solo was unplanned: session ace Louie Shelton played it on a Fender Telecaster through a 1969 Fender Princeton Reverb amp and an inexpensive Boss distortion pedal.
Radio broke it by accident: a Cleveland R&B DJ started playing 'Lowdown' straight off the album, listener response was so positive that Columbia shipped it to R&B stations, then Top 40 followed.
Scaggs called its success 'an accident' — he and the musicians thought there 'wasn't a chance in hell' it would be released as a single, even though it was their favorite track on the album.
When it did become a single in June 1976, it hit No. 1 on the Cash Box Top 100, No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100, No. 5 on both the R&B and disco charts, and No. 2 in Canada.
The single was certified Gold by the RIAA for a million copies sold, and the album version runs 5:16 — more than two minutes longer than the 3:14 single edit, with 'Harbor Lights' on the flip side.
Grammy glory: 'Lowdown' won Best R&B Song at the 19th Annual Grammy Awards in 1977, an honor shared by its two writers, Scaggs and Paich.
Second lives: Scaggs re-recorded it as an unplugged jazz number for his 1996 album Fade Into Light, and in 2020 Disclosure sampled it for their track 'Expressing What Matters.'

title: Lowdown

description: Flight of the Conchords' Bret McKenzie goes sincere: an '80s-glow tribute to late engineer Dave Bianco and his North Hollywood studio, from solo debut Songs Without Jokes (2022).

pops.text: It's track three on Songs Without Jokes, McKenzie's full-length solo debut, released August 26, 2022, through Sub Pop — the same label behind Flight of the Conchords.
Preview duty: 'Dave's Place' arrived in June 2022 as the album's second advance single, following the lead track 'A Little Tune.'
Humble start: McKenzie wrote it, in his words, 'one night at home in Wellington while strumming away on my guitar,' then developed it in Los Angeles with producer Mickey Petralia.
Genre swerve: what started as a three-chord country song 'came out the other side an eighties Blade Runner, Dire Straits-esque jam,' as McKenzie himself describes the transformation.
The Dave in the title is Dave Bianco, an audio engineer McKenzie had worked with on various occasions in Los Angeles.
Bianco had a studio in North Hollywood that he himself referred to as 'Dave's place' — and the song is named after that room.
Bianco died not long before McKenzie started making the record. McKenzie finally worked at Dave's studio after he passed, and this track came out of that session.
'I sometimes think Dave is watching over this one,' McKenzie said of the song — a sincere tribute from a musician famous for comedy songs.
The album was produced by Petralia and McKenzie, recorded at East West Studios and United Recordings, mixed by Darrell Thorpe and mastered by Dave Ives at 101 Mastering in Los Angeles.
On stage it grew: McKenzie performed the song live in September 2022 at Auckland Town Hall with an eight-piece band of Wellington musicians, and later brought it to CBS Saturday Morning.

title: Dave's Place

description: Reckless opens at full throttle: Bryan Adams and Jim Vallance's one-night-stand rocker, the album's fifth single and its only one never given a music video. It still hit No. 13.

pops.text: Track one, side one: this is the opening song on Reckless, Adams's fourth studio album — and it still had to wait its turn, coming out as the album's fifth single.
Adams wrote it with his longtime songwriting partner Jim Vallance, and it was recorded in April 1984 at Little Mountain Sound Studios in Vancouver.
Birthday release: Reckless came out on November 5, 1984 — Adams's 25th birthday — and went on to become his only album to top the US Billboard 200.
No video, no problem: of the six singles released from Reckless, this was the only one never given a music video.
Canada heard it first: the song went to Canadian radio in February 1985, months before its September 1985 release as a US single.
Chart peak: it reached No. 13 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 7 on the Top Rock Tracks chart, and No. 19 in Canada — making it, remarkably, the lowest-charting of the six Reckless singles.
That context is wild: every one of Reckless's six singles reached the top 20 of the Hot 100, a hit rate few rock albums of the era could match.
Movie moment: the song turns up in the 1985 sci-fi comedy Real Genius, starring Val Kilmer, during the Tanning Invitational pool-party scene.

Running joke: co-writer Jim Vallance says that when guitarist Keith Scott first heard the song, they swapped the lyric to 'if the night was made for love, it ain't for Keith' — and Adams still sings it that way to him live.
Keepers' shelf: the song earned a place on Adams's 2005 compilation Anthology, his career-spanning two-disc retrospective.

title: One Night Love Affair
